findings.title: Hardcoded credential: aws access key id
findings.description: A value matching the `aws-access-key-id` pattern was found committed in source. Secrets in version control are exposed to everyone with repository access and remain in history even after removal.
findings.why_vulnerable: A credential is committed in source, so anyone with repository access (or a leaked copy) obtains it.
findings.attacker_perspective: Read the value straight from version control history and use it directly against the corresponding service.
findings.business_impact: Unauthorized access to the associated account or service, and any data or spend it controls.

remediation.summary: Remove the secret from source and rotate it.
remediation.guidance:
1. Revoke/rotate the exposed credential now, assume it is compromised.
2. Move the value to a secret manager or an environment variable loaded at runtime.
3. Purge it from git history (e.g. git-filter-repo) so it is not recoverable.
4. Add a pre-commit secret scan to prevent recurrence.

evidence.basis: The value matches a provider's exact key format; it was not checked with the provider.
verify: Open app.py line 2 and read the flagged code.
Check whether the value is a real credential or a placeholder, sample or test value.
If it is real, rotate it with the provider and remove it from the repository history.
Confirm the reason given applies here: A credential is committed in source, so anyone with repository access (or a leaked copy) obtains it.

findings.title: SQL injection (tainted value reaches a database query)
findings.description: A value derived from untrusted input flows into a database query without parameterization, so input can change the query's structure.
findings.why_vulnerable: A value derived from untrusted input flows into a database query without parameterization, so input can change the query's structure.
findings.attacker_perspective: Supply `' OR '1'='1` (or a UNION/stacked query) in the tainted parameter to read or modify unintended rows.
findings.business_impact: Unauthorized data access or modification, up to full database compromise.

remediation.summary: Use parameterized queries / bound parameters and never build SQL from input, even across intermediate variables.
remediation.guidance: Use parameterized queries / bound parameters and never build SQL from input, even across intermediate variables.

evidence.basis: Request data reaches the SQL call with no recognized sanitizer on the path.

path.code: query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = '" + uid + "'"

verify: Open web.py line 9 and confirm the value read there comes from the request.
Follow it through lines 9 and 10 and check that nothing validates, escapes or converts it before web.py line 13.
Check whether any caller, decorator or middleware validates the value before web.py line 13.
In a test environment you own, pass a value containing a single quote (for example ' OR '1'='1) and check whether the query fails or returns other rows.

findings.title: Attack chain: injection foothold beside an exposed credential
findings.description:
This component contains both a hardcoded credential and an injection vulnerability. An attacker exploiting the injection gains code or query execution in the very component that holds the secret, so a single foothold yields both execution and a credential for lateral movement.

Chained findings: secrets.aws-access-key-id (app.py:2); patterns.python-shell-true (app.py:4)
findings.why_vulnerable: This component contains both a hardcoded credential and an injection vulnerability. An attacker exploiting the injection gains code or query execution in the very component that holds the secret, so a single foothold yields both execution and a credential for lateral movement.
findings.attacker_perspective: Individually these findings look moderate; chained, each one enables the next, so an attacker can walk the entire path from untrusted input to impact.
findings.business_impact: Compounded impact: the chain reaches a materially worse outcome than any single finding in it.

remediation.summary: Break the chain: fixing any one link stops this path, fix all for defense in depth.
remediation.guidance: Breaking the weakest link is enough to stop this specific path, but address every chained finding so a variant cannot re-open it.

findings.title: Unsafe yaml.load without SafeLoader
findings.description: yaml.load with the default loader can construct arbitrary Python objects from the document.
findings.why_vulnerable: yaml.load with the default loader can construct arbitrary Python objects from the document.
findings.attacker_perspective: Feed a YAML payload using `!!python/object/apply` tags to execute code.

remediation.patch:
--- a/app.py
+++ b/app.py
@@ -11 +11 @@
-    return yaml.load(s)
+    return yaml.safe_load(s)

evidence.basis: A pattern or heuristic match; the tool did not show that attacker-controlled data reaches this code.
verify: Open app.py line 11 and read the flagged code.
Check where the values used on that line come from; it is a risk only if an attacker can influence them.
Check whether the serialized data can come from outside; never load untrusted samples outside a sandbox.
Confirm the reason given applies here: yaml.load with the default loader can construct arbitrary Python objects from the document.

findings.title: Command execution with shell=True
findings.description: Running a subprocess through the shell lets shell metacharacters in any interpolated input execute additional commands.
findings.why_vulnerable: Running a subprocess through the shell lets shell metacharacters in any interpolated input execute additional commands.
findings.attacker_perspective: Provide input containing `; rm -rf /` or `$(...)` to run arbitrary commands as the app user.
findings.business_impact: Remote code execution on the host.

remediation.summary: Pass the command as an argument list without shell=True, and validate/escape any external input.
remediation.guidance: Pass the command as an argument list without shell=True, and validate/escape any external input.
remediation.patch:
--- a/app.py
+++ b/app.py
@@ -4 +4 @@
-    subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True)
+    subprocess.run(cmd, shell=False)

evidence.basis: A pattern or heuristic match; the tool did not show that attacker-controlled data reaches this code.
verify: Open app.py line 4 and read the flagged code.
Check where the values used on that line come from; it is a risk only if an attacker can influence them.
In a test environment you own, pass a value that adds a harmless second command after a semicolon and check whether it runs.
Confirm the reason given applies here: Running a subprocess through the shell lets shell metacharacters in any interpolated input execute additional commands.

findings.title: Sensitive route may lack authentication: /user
findings.description: Route `/user` matches sensitive path patterns and has no obvious auth decorator or Depends() in the surrounding code.
findings.why_vulnerable: Administrative or sensitive endpoints without authentication allow unauthenticated access.
findings.attacker_perspective: Call the endpoint directly without credentials.
findings.business_impact: Unauthorized access to privileged functionality or data.

remediation.guidance: Add framework-native auth (Depends(get_current_user), @login_required, middleware) before handler logic.

evidence.basis: A pattern or heuristic match; the tool did not show that attacker-controlled data reaches this code.

findings.title: Weak hash algorithm (MD5/SHA1)
findings.description: MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security purposes (collisions, speed) and must not be used for integrity or password hashing.
findings.why_vulnerable: MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security purposes (collisions, speed) and must not be used for integrity or password hashing.
findings.attacker_perspective: Exploit collision weaknesses, or brute-force fast hashes for stored passwords.
findings.business_impact: Forged signatures/integrity checks, or recovered passwords.

remediation.summary: Use SHA-256+ for integrity and a slow KDF (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2) for passwords.
remediation.guidance: Use SHA-256+ for integrity and a slow KDF (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2) for passwords.
remediation.patch:
--- a/app.py
+++ b/app.py
@@ -6 +6 @@
-    return hashlib.md5(x).hexdigest()
+    return hashlib.sha256(x).hexdigest()

evidence.basis: A pattern or heuristic match; the tool did not show that attacker-controlled data reaches this code.
verify: Open app.py line 6 and read the flagged code.
Check where the values used on that line come from; it is a risk only if an attacker can influence them.
Confirm the reason given applies here: MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security purposes (collisions, speed) and must not be used for integrity or password hashing.

findings.title: SQL query built by string formatting from a non-constant value
findings.description: The query passed to execute() is assembled with %, + , .format() or an f-string from a value that is not a constant. No untrusted source was traced to it in this file, but if the value can be influenced by a caller (a function parameter, a request elsewhere), the query structure can change.

location.snippet: cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + uid)

findings.why_vulnerable: The query passed to execute() is assembled with %, + , .format() or an f-string from a value that is not a constant. No untrusted source was traced to it in this file, but if the value can be influenced by a caller (a function parameter, a request elsewhere), the query structure can change.
findings.attacker_perspective: If any caller passes attacker-controlled text, inject SQL through it.
findings.business_impact: Unauthorized data access or modification if the value is attacker-controlled.

remediation.summary: Pass values as bound parameters (execute(sql, params)) instead of formatting them into the SQL text.
remediation.guidance: Pass values as bound parameters (execute(sql, params)) instead of formatting them into the SQL text.
